extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, actors and drama instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and teaching principles for theatrical improvisation and comic performance, covering status work, spontaneity, blocking/accepting, narrative technique, space, masks/trance, and exercises for classes. Aimed at producing effective improvisers and training students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Try to get your status just a little above or below your partner's,' I said, and I insisted that the gap should be minimal. The actors seemed to know exactly what I meant and the work was transformed. ... Suddenly we understood that every inflection and movement implies a status, and that no action is due to chance, or really 'motiveless'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status is something one does: you may be low in social status, but play high, and vice versa. Teach actors to be aware that every inflection, movement, voice and posture implies status. Use status to make scenes authentic; notice that friends 'play' status games together. Status transactions continue all the time; avoid assuming status only exists in conflict. Practical examples: minimal status gap, use of teasing/insults to shift status, observe how 'friendly' remarks may imply hostile status. Tragedy/comedy use status differently (sacrifice raises status before death; most comedy lowers status).

rubrics_metrics.name: See-saw principle (raising/lowering status)
rubrics_metrics.description: We soon discovered the 'see-saw' principle: 'I go up and you go down'. If I'm trying to lower my end of the see-saw, and my mind blocks, I can always switch to raising the other end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach actors to switch between raising themselves and lowering their partners in alternate sentences and vice versa. Most comedy works on the see-saw principle: a comedian is someone paid to lower his own or other people's status. Use examples (Ken Dodd patter) to show how self-lowering combined with manic behavior absolves audience sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching status (exercises and cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: I ask a group to mill about and say 'hallo' to each other. ... I then get some of the group to hold all eye contacts for a couple of seconds, while the others try to make and then break eye contacts and then immediately glance back for a moment. ... Those who hold eye contacts report that they feel powerful-and actually look powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical exercises: milling and greeting, controlled eye-contact holds/breaks, head stillness for authority, precise timing of glance lengths. Watch for resistances: some students always play low status and won't hold eye contact; high-status students may hold glance-back too long. Teachers must control lengths and understand subconscious resistance. Use playful insults (non-personal) or props (custard pies) to help students accept humiliation and loosen up. Remove responsibility for choice of insult to reduce personal hurt. For authority roles, teach still-head technique and sustained eye contact. Observe student reports to adjust exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space (proxemics)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I stand two students face to face and about a foot apart they're likely to feel a strong desire to change their body position. ... High-status players ... will allow their space to flow into other people. Low-status players will avoid letting their space flow into other people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical proximity to generate emotional responses: letting 'space' flow produces dominance; shutting off space (kneeling, bowing) is ritualised low-status. To humiliate, refuse to let a low-status person switch off their space (stand an inch from face and scream). Teach actors to notice how space-streaming creates feelings of love/hate. Use space deliberately to create status effects onstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity (cultivating unthought responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an improviser is stuck for an idea, he shouldn't search for one, he should trigger his partner's ability to give 'unthought' answers. ... If you don't know what to do in a scene, just say something like, 'Oh my God! What's that?' This immediately jerks images into your partner's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage an environment like a party rather than a formal classroom; avoid puritanical suppression of students' impulses. Teach partners to trigger unpremeditated responses. Use exercises that distract or overload the censor (e.g., write a paragraph while counting backward) to bypass self-censorship. Emphasize that imagination should be effortless and that fear of being wrong or obscene often blocks spontaneity. Reassure students they're not responsible for content; misdirect responsibility to free them, then later restore responsibility when they are stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (accept first thoughts; be obvious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many students block their imaginations because they're afraid of being unoriginal. ... The improviser has to realise that the more obvious he is, the more original he appears. ... An artist who is inspired is being obvious. He's not making any decisions, he's not weighing one idea against another. He's accepting his first thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train performers to accept first, obvious ideas rather than overthinking. Encourage 'yes' responses (yeasayers) instead of 'no' blocking (naysayers). Use examples (Fred Karno pen trick) to test willingness to accept and play along. You can train naysayers to behave like yeasayers by exercises that reward affirmation and spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking and Accepting (offers and blocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: I call anything that an actor does an 'offer'. Each offer can either be accepted, or blocked. ... A block is anything that prevents the action from developing, or that wipes out your partner's premise. ... Scenes spontaneously generate themselves if both actors offer and accept alternately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define offers, accepts, and blocks; emphasize acceptance as the mechanism that generates action. Teach that blocking is a form of aggression and that good improvisers accept offers (including accidental ones) to maintain flow. Use exercises where actors practice accepting physical/comedic offers. Explain life-application: people's life events are shaped by patterns of blocking and yielding. Use Stanislavsky example of continuing after an accident to teach acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind Offers (intentionless gestures game)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you make a blind offer, you have no intention to communicate at all. Your partner accepts the offer, and you say 'Thank you.' Then he makes an intentionless gesture, and you accept that, and he says 'Thank you' and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise procedure: make a gesture that moves away from the body, freeze until partner reacts; accept each blind offer with 'Thank you'. Later play the game while discussing a different subject to create telepathic-looking interactions. Audience response: the ritualized 'Thank you' and the unexpected gestures are highly entertaining. Use this game to build trust and improvisational responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative skills (walking backwards, interrupting routines, reincorporation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The improviser has to be like a man walking backwards. He sees where he has been, but he pays no attention to the future. ... As a story progresses it begins to establish other routines and these in their turn have to be broken. ... The rules are: (1) interrupt a routine; (2) keep the action onstage - don't get diverted on to an action that has happened elsewhere, or at some other time; (3) don't cancel the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: 'walk backwards' — remember and reincorporate earlier shelved incidents to give shape and pleasure to audiences. Use 'interrupting routines' to generate narrative (deliberately describe a routine then interrupt it). Keep action onstage and avoid cancelling the story. Group exercises: groups of three invent a character together and agree fully (not compromise) to build backstory and traits. Use distraction/overload to bypass censor for narrative material. Teach students to reincorporate earlier material for audience gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masks and Trance (inducing trance/persona)
rubrics_metrics.description: It's true that an actor can wear a Mask casually, and just pretend to be another person, but Gaskill and myself were absolutely clear that we were trying to induce trance states. ... If you lie down and make your body relax, going through it from feet to head, and loosening any points of tension that you find, then you easily float away into fantasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Masks (capital 'M') and relaxation to induce trance states in which performers are 'inhabited' by a spirit; practice progressive relaxation from feet to head to float into fantasy. Understand cultural resistance to trance and how anonymity in crowds facilitates trance. Note that normal, well-adjusted people are often most suggestible. Encourage practices that reduce 'personality' guarding (e.g., convincing students they're not responsible for actions) to allow trance and mask work. Exercise caution: create safe environments and be aware of psychological effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yeasayers vs Naysayers (psychological disposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'naysayers' and its opposite, 'yeasayers' ... Yeasayers seem to be 'id-dominated' personalities ... The naysayer wants to maintain inner equilibrium ... The naysayer's general attitude is one of stimulus rejection - a pervasive unwillingness to respond to impulsive or environmental forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize performers' default orientation: yeasayers readily accept and respond (low psychological inertia) and are naturally good at improvisation; naysayers censor and block. Teaching strategy: identify naysayers and use targeted exercises to reduce censorship and increase stimulus acceptance; use overload, play-party atmosphere, and specific acceptance drills to train naysayers toward yeasayer behaviors.
